fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for a sound that lacks low-frequency energy, weight and power, coming across as thin, weak and underpowered with little punch or body.
fields.plain_english: A gutless sound is weak and thin. It has almost no bass or punch, so it feels small and lacks power.
fields.purpose_function: Gives engineers a quick shared term for a tonal balance that is short on lows and low-mids, pointing toward more level, low-end support, or a fuller source.
fields.practical_application: A tech might call a bass DI 'gutless' and add low-mid EQ, re-amp it, or swap to a fuller-sounding source to restore weight.
common_mistakes: Confusing gutless (lack of low-end power) with thin (lack of body across the low-mids) and treating them the same.
Trying to fix a gutless sound only with volume instead of restoring the missing low-frequency content.
Boosting deep sub-bass to compensate, which adds rumble without the punch that was actually missing.
scenario_contexts: A bass guitar DI that sounds gutless in the mix and needs low-mid support.
A kick drum that lacks weight and punch through a small PA.
A vocal that sounds gutless and underpowered next to a dense backing track.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for an unpleasant, aggressive, edgy quality, usually caused by excess energy or distortion in the upper-midrange/presence region (roughly 2-5 kHz), that is fatiguing to listen to.
fields.plain_english: A harsh sound is rough and hard on the ears. It has too much high-mid energy, so it feels sharp and tiring to hear.
fields.purpose_function: Flags a specific tonal fault so engineers know to look for a peak, resonance or distortion in the presence band and tame it.
fields.practical_application: An engineer hearing a harsh cymbal or vocal will sweep a narrow EQ cut through 2-5 kHz, check for clipping, or ease off a compressor or exciter to smooth it out.
common_mistakes: Confusing harsh (aggressive upper-mid/presence energy) with bright (extended but pleasant highs).
Cutting broad high frequencies and dulling the whole source instead of finding the narrow offending band.
Blaming the source when the harshness is actually clipping or distortion somewhere in the gain chain.
scenario_contexts: A vocal that turns harsh on loud notes through a PA.
Cymbals or an electric guitar amp that sound harsh on a bright console.
A cheap microphone or converter adding a harsh edge to a recording.

fields.definition: Short for high fidelity; reproduction that closely and accurately matches the original source, with wide, even frequency response, low distortion and low noise. As a timbre descriptor, a clean, detailed, full-range and refined sound.
fields.plain_english: Hi-fi is short for high fidelity. It means the sound is clean, clear, and true to the real thing. It has full lows and highs with very little noise.
fields.purpose_function: Serves as a benchmark of accurate, faithful reproduction against which colored or degraded 'lo-fi' sounds are judged.
fields.practical_application: A tech describes a monitor chain or recording as hi-fi when it is clean, extended and uncolored, or deliberately degrades a track toward lo-fi for effect.
common_mistakes: Assuming hi-fi just means loud or bass-heavy rather than accurate and low in distortion.
Confusing a 'hyped', exciting sound with true high fidelity.
Judging fidelity on colored consumer speakers instead of accurate monitors.
scenario_contexts: Describing a mastering monitor chain that reproduces sources cleanly and accurately.
Comparing a hi-fi full-range recording against a deliberately lo-fi effected track.
Evaluating whether a converter or preamp adds coloration or stays hi-fi.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for a tone with a scooped or notched midrange and resonant coloration, giving a distant, cupped, tube-like quality; often the result of a midrange dip, phase cancellation or comb filtering.
fields.plain_english: A hollow sound is missing its middle tones. It sounds far away and cupped, like someone talking into a tube or barrel.
fields.purpose_function: Points to a midrange deficiency or comb-filter coloration so engineers can check mic placement, polarity and EQ.
fields.practical_application: Hearing a hollow snare or vocal, a tech checks for phase cancellation between mics, corrects polarity or placement, and restores midrange with EQ.
common_mistakes: Fixing a hollow, comb-filtered sound with EQ alone instead of correcting mic phase or placement.
Confusing hollow (scooped mids) with boxy (excess low-mids).
Scooping the mids on purpose and then wondering why the source sits poorly in the mix.
scenario_contexts: Two mics on one source combining out of phase and sounding hollow.
A vocal that sounds hollow and distant after a midrange cut.
A snare recorded in a way that produces a hollow, tube-like tone.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for a nasal, midrange-heavy coloration with excess energy roughly in the 500 Hz-1 kHz range, resembling speech through cupped hands or a megaphone.
fields.plain_english: A honky sound is nasal and pinched. It sounds like someone talking through cupped hands, with too much middle honk.
fields.purpose_function: Identifies an over-prominent lower-midrange resonance so it can be located and cut with EQ.
fields.practical_application: An engineer tames a honky acoustic guitar or vocal by sweeping a narrow EQ cut through 500 Hz-1 kHz until the nasal quality clears.
common_mistakes: Confusing honky (around 500 Hz-1 kHz emphasis) with boxy (lower, around 300-600 Hz emphasis).
Cutting too wide and hollowing out the midrange instead of notching the honk.
Assuming the honk is the source when it is a room or enclosure resonance.
scenario_contexts: An acoustic guitar that sounds honky through a piezo pickup.
A vocal mic with a midrange resonance that sounds honky.
A small speaker or wedge with a honky midrange bump.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for a sound with a deliberately exaggerated, non-flat frequency response, typically boosted lows and highs with scooped mids ('smile' EQ), that sounds exciting and enhanced rather than accurate.
fields.plain_english: A hyped sound has boosted lows and highs and scooped middles. It sounds exciting at first, but it is not a true, flat picture of the music.
fields.purpose_function: Names an enhanced, flattering tonal balance so engineers can tell an impressive-sounding presentation from a true, flat one.
fields.practical_application: A tech recognizes hyped consumer speakers or a hyped mix and cross-checks decisions on flat monitors so the balance translates elsewhere.
common_mistakes: Mixing on hyped speakers and making a dull, thin mix that only sounds right on those speakers.
Confusing a hyped, exciting sound with an accurate one.
Adding hype with EQ on every channel until the mix is fatiguing and cluttered.
scenario_contexts: Consumer earbuds or a boombox with a hyped, smiling response.
A demo playback system voiced hyped to impress clients.
A mix bus that has been hyped with too much high and low boost.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for an extremely piercing, painful high-frequency peak, often around 3-8 kHz, that feels like a sharp stab in the ears; a severe, localized form of harshness.
fields.plain_english: An ice-pick sound has a sharp, piercing high note that stabs your ears. It is a very painful, extreme kind of harshness.
fields.purpose_function: Flags a narrow, painful treble resonance so it can be found and notched out before it causes listener discomfort.
fields.practical_application: Hearing an ice-pick peak on cymbals or a vocal, a tech sweeps a narrow boosted EQ to locate the frequency, then cuts it sharply.
common_mistakes: Cutting a wide band and dulling the whole top end instead of notching the narrow ice-pick frequency.
Confusing ice-pick (a narrow, piercing peak) with general brightness.
UNSAFE: Enduring an ice-pick peak at high monitoring levels, risking ear fatigue and hearing damage instead of cutting it.
scenario_contexts: A cymbal or hi-hat with an ice-pick peak on a bright PA.
A vocal sibilance region that stabs at a specific high frequency.
A resonant tweeter or horn producing an ice-pick tone.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for a closed-in, boxy coloration in which the sound seems enclosed, caused by excess low-midrange resonance (roughly 300-600 Hz) and a lack of openness and air.
fields.plain_english: A sound 'in a box' feels closed-in and boxy. It has too much low-middle tone, like the music is trapped inside a small box.
fields.purpose_function: Identifies a low-mid buildup and lack of top-end openness so engineers can cut the boxiness and add air.
fields.practical_application: A tech cuts around 300-600 Hz and may add a gentle high-frequency lift to open up a source that sounds 'in a box'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'in a box' (low-mid boxiness, around 300-600 Hz) with honky (higher, around 500 Hz-1 kHz).
Boosting highs to 'open it up' without cutting the low-mid buildup causing the boxiness.
Overlooking that a small, untreated room or enclosure is adding the boxy resonance.
scenario_contexts: A vocal recorded in a small untreated room that sounds in a box.
A guitar cabinet close-mic'd in a way that produces a boxy, closed-in tone.
A conference or podcast mic in a reflective space sounding in a box.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for a very present, forward and immediate sound that seems close to the listener, usually from strong presence-region energy, high directness and little room ambience.
fields.plain_english: An in-your-face sound is bold, close, and upfront. It feels like the music is right in front of you, with little room echo.
fields.purpose_function: Describes a forward, upfront presentation so engineers can dial presence, dryness and level to place a source aggressively in the mix.
fields.practical_application: To make a vocal in-your-face, a tech boosts presence, keeps it dry and compressed, and raises it forward in the balance.
common_mistakes: Pushing every element in-your-face so nothing has depth or sits back in the mix.
Confusing in-your-face (forward and present) with simply loud.
Adding so much presence to be upfront that the source becomes harsh.
scenario_contexts: A lead vocal mixed dry and forward to sound in-your-face.
A rock guitar meant to be aggressive and upfront.
A voiceover kept in-your-face for impact in a commercial.
